whatItDoes: Re-saves PDFs with optimized object streams via pdf-lib to reduce size 5–15% without rasterizing. Shows original vs new size, saved bytes, compression ratio, page count, and lets you download the optimized file. All client-side.
whyItExists: PDFs often contain uncompressed object streams. Re-saving with `useObjectStreams: false` and compact content can shave payload without quality loss, locally without uploading to a server that might keep your document.
whoShouldUse: Anyone needing to email or upload a PDF that is slightly too large, and who wants a private, no-upload optimization before trying heavier image recompression.
useCases: Shrink a 5MB 20-page PDF by re-saving with object streams
Compare original vs compressed size before deciding to recompress images separately
instructions: Drop a PDF (10MB). The tool shows page count and original size.
Pick quality (low/medium/high — currently re-save only, UI for future image recompression).
Click Compress — the tool copies pages to a new PDFDocument and saves with optimized streams.
Download the compressed PDF from the green card showing saved bytes and ratio.
examples: Input: 10-page PDF 5.0MB → Output: 4.6MB (saved 400KB, 8% reduction) via object stream optimization.
Input: 1-page PDF with many fonts → Output: similar size if already optimized; ratio near 0% is expected.
bestPractices: Try this first before image-based compressors — it is lossless and fast
If ratio is 0%, your PDF is already optimized; try Image Compressor on extracted images instead
commonMistakes: Expecting 50% reduction — this method only optimizes structure, not images; use image tools for heavy cuts
Uploading encrypted PDFs — pdf-lib will error; remove password first
faq: Is the PDF uploaded? No — compression is pdf-lib in your browser. Files never leave your device.
Does it recompress images? Not yet — currently structural optimization only. Image recompression is on the roadmap.
Will it preserve text? Yes — pages are copied vector-for-vector, not rasterized.
features: Original vs compressed size and ratio
